Scotland’s ramped-up second-half performance offered some cause for optimism as Sébastien Pocognoli’s tenure as head coach began with a goalless draw with Slovenia in Ljubljana.

The 39-year-old Belgian head coach, appointed in August as Steve Clarke’s successor, refreshed the side for the Nations League Group B1 opener in the Stozice Stadium, but they were fortunate on a couple of occasions at least not to fall behind before rallying before the break.

Scotland had been insipid and uninspiring for most of the first half but after the interval they played with pace and purpose as Slovenia captain and goalkeeper Jan Oblak became a key figure, making saves from Oli McBurnie and Kieron Bowie.

Oli McBurnie spurns a chance for Scotland.It remains goalless between Slovenia and Scotland.📺 Watch on BBC One pic.twitter.com/sldzhNCGGb.

“It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play,” McBurnie told BBC Scotland.

In a recent development, “We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored. I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

According to recent reports, “Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

However, the goal that would have made the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager’s debut as an international boss more memorable ultimately failed to arrive.

In this extended international break, the Scots will host Switzerland at Hampden on Tuesday and then travel to North Macedonia before taking on Slovenia in Glasgow, with the Tartan Army hoping to see further improvement – and goals.

September 29: Scotland vs Switzerland.

October 3: North Macedonia vs Scotland.

October 6: Scotland vs Slovenia.

November 13: Scotland vs North Macedonia.

November 16: Switzerland vs Scotland.

Speaking to BBC Scotland, the debutant stated: “Thought we struggled to get into the game first half, but second half we completely dominated the game.

“They’ve got a top goalie who made really good saves. So many positives to take and a clean sheet as well.

“We changed shape a wee bit at half-time to get more control and that did really well for us.

“It’s a big game again on Tuesday so it’s crucial to recover now and go again.

“I’ve played on the left-hand side for a couple of years now, so I’m comfortable doing that.

“We’ve had a great week. A new manager, new way of playing and new faces in camp. It’s just the chances we need to take - the fact we’re creating the chances stands us in good stead.”.

The striker told BBC Scotland: “It took us a bit of getting used to in the first half, the way the gaffer wants to play.

“We created enough chances to win the game. I should have scored.

Sources indicate that “I was asked to play a different position and I enjoyed it. I’d rather be getting in the positions than not getting chances.

“Second half was a lot more of what the manager wanted from us. It was waves of pressure and the only thing missing was a goal or two.”.

Pocognoli’s first game in charge of Scotland ends in a goalless draw. The visitors produced a dominant second-half display, but their final ball and end-product was severely lacking in crucial moments. Ure, Hickey, Gilmour, McBurnie and Bowie all came close to scoring, but no one could break the deadlock.

According to recent reports, scotland cannot find a way past the impenetrable Oblak. There will be just two minutes of added time for the visitors to possibly score a late winner.

Sources indicate that lovric clatters into Gilmour and is cautioned. Slovenia can’t get out. It’s wave after wave of Scottish pressure.

Oblak comes out and fails to claim Robertson’s free-kick. The ball is recycled and the Tottenham full-back whips a second cross into the box and Slovenia fail to clear. Welsh is waiting for it, but lashes a first-time volley over the bar.

Karnicnik catches Robertson with a late lunging tackle and receives a yellow card, giving Scotland a chance to get the ball into the box.

The hosts make their fifth alteration of the afternoon, with Cerin withdrawn and Lovric on instead.

It has been revealed that how has Bowie missed?! Gilmour finds Bowie with an outstanding pass through the centre of Slovenia’s defence. The substitute takes a touch then scuffs a rushed finish wide. Bowie has to do better there!

Another change is here for Scotland, with Gannon-Doak on to replace Hickey.

The hosts make another double change as Sporar and Brekalo depart for Vipotnik and Balkovec.

Sources indicate that welsh spots Bowie’s run and threads a perfectly-weighted pass through to the forward. From an unfavourable angle, the substitute’s one-on-one attempt is blocked by Oblak.

Gilmour and McBurnie play a devastating one-two, allowing the midfielder to advance into the penalty area. He shoots and aims for the far corner, but his placed effort is collected impressively by Oblak, who makes another crucial intervention.

The second half has started as the first ended, with Scotland applying all of the pressure. Slovenia have Oblak to thank for the goalless scoreline.

McBurnie and Oblak both challenge for the ball, with the Scotsman bumping into the goalkeeper, giving Slovenia a goal kick. The decision is met by a chorus of boos from the away fans.

Upon reflection, it looks like McBurnie should have just shot and tried to put the ball between Oblak’s legs. He did the hard part, but lacked a clinical finish.

Can they produce a more inspired second-half performance?

On paper, it looks like Sebastien Pocognoli has opted for a five-back formation, with Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh making his Scotland debut as one of the centre backs.

Captain Andy Robertson and Brentford’s Aaron Hickey will operate as the wing-backs, with Billy Gilmour, Lewis Ferguson and John McGinn forming a midfield three.

A new-look attack is spearheaded by the returning Oli McBurnie and 22-year-old Robbie Ure, who like Welsh, will also make his Scotland debut.

Angus Gunn remains his country’s first-choice goalkeeper.

Industry observers note that “We need to create a good energy but it’s up to us on the pitch to create this. So then we can be hand in hand with the supporters.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this UEFA Nations League B, Group 1 match as Slovenia host Scotland at Stozice Stadium in Ljubljana.

It has been revealed that scotland qualified for their first World Cup in 28 years this summer, but they exited the tournament with a whimper after failing to finish as one of the best third-place group sides. Steve Clarke’s men beat tournament debutants Haiti 1-0 in their opening match, before falling to defeats without scoring against Morocco and Brazil.

Sources indicate that following the World Cup, Clarke stepped down as Scotland’s head coach, ending a seven-year tenure, and was replaced by Belgian manager Sebastien Pocognoli. The former Monaco boss will take charge of his first game in his new role today and will be itching to make an encouraging start in a new era for Scottish football.

Over this extended international break, Pocognoli’s side will also face Switzerland and North Macedonia, as well as a return fixture against Slovenia in Scotland on October 6 to round off a busy period.

While Scotland took part in the World Cup, Slovenia were reflecting on their hugely disappointing qualification performance, where they finished third in their group behind Switzerland and Kosovo without winning and netting just three goals across six matches.

Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko – Slovenia’s star man and most well-known player – withdrew from Bostjan Cesar’s squad earlier this week after the recurrence of a shin injury caused the 23-year-old to completely miss the 1-1 draw against Fulham last Sunday.

Scotland have a few notable absences, with Scott McTominay, Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland all unavailable, but Billy Gilmour returns to the fold after missing the World Cup through injury, Oli McBurnie has been recalled and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure has received his first senior call-up.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adepoju Marvellous | 26 Nov 2026 18:20, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 19:56.

High-flying Cambuur will look to continue their resurgence when they host Sparta Rotterdam at Kooi Stadion on Saturday evening.

On the other hand, the visitors head to Leeuwarden aiming to end a run of consecutive defeats and arrest a slump in form which has seen them lose four of their last five matches.

Like fellow newcomers ADO Den Haag and Willem II, Cambuur made a difficult start to life back in the top flight, collecting just one point from their opening five matches before claiming their first win of the season against NEC on September 12.

According to recent reports, johan Plat’s men have barely looked back since. Saturday’s 3-2 victory over Utrecht was their sixth win in nine matches across all competitions (D2, L1), the second-best record in the division over that period, behind only Ajax.

Now eighth in the Eredivisie table, the Yellow-Blues are closer to the European places than the relegation zone - a prospect that seemed inconceivable after they opened the campaign with four straight defeats by a combined score of 16-4.

Only seven of Cambuur’s 18 points so far have come in home matches, leaving them with much improvement in front of their fans, where November 8’s 5-2 thrashing at the hands of reigning champions PSV Eindhoven marked a fourth defeat in seven outings this term.

Saturday’s hosts are also winless in their last five home matches against Sparta dating back to January 2026 and could only muster one point across both meetings of their most recent Eredivisie campaign in 2022-23, leaving further room for apprehension within the home crowd.

After winning five consecutive Eredivisie matches either side of the new year, Sparta would have been optimistic about 2026. However, following a tumultuous couple of months, they will now be desperate to avoid ending the year in the bottom three.

Appointed to steady the ship following the departure of long-serving manager Maurice Steijn, Rogier Meijer has yet to spark a turnaround at Het Kasteel, and the former NEC boss is under increasing pressure to improve results.

Sunday’s 5-1 defeat to AZ Alkmaar was Meijer’s heaviest since taking charge in July, with Sparta having now conceded at least twice in 11 consecutive matches, giving them the division’s third-worst defensive record behind Willem II and FC Utrecht.

Only Groningen and Utrecht have scored more than De Rood-Witte Gladiatoren’s 22 goals among the bottom-half teams, so finding the net has not been a problem for Sparta and reducing their defensive frailties could help spark an upturn in form.

In the second of two consecutive away matches against newly-promoted sides, Saturday’s visitors will look to respond to a disappointing 3-1 defeat to ADO Den Haag last time out.

Sparta have scored four of their 15 away goals between the 15th and 30th minute, while Cambuur have conceded seven of their 20 home goals during the same period, giving Meijer’s men a prime window of opportunity to strike.

Jamal Amofa is expected to miss the rest of the season after suffering a cruciate ligament injury in October.

Twenty-four-year-old Jorn Berkhout was left out of the matchday squad against Utrecht due to injury, making his involvement on Saturday uncertain.

Nicolas Binder and Ilyes Hamache have each scored in three of Cambuur’s last five league matches and will be key to the hosts’ attacking threat.

Bruno Martins Indi is ineligible to feature for Sparta after he was sent off for two bookable offences six minutes apart against AZ.

He joins fellow defenders Teo Quintero and Nick Verschuren as the visitors continue to suffer from defensive absentees, which have plagued their season to date.

First-choice goalkeeper Michael Brouwer was absent last time out, so Filip Bednarek, who is averaging a 52% save accuracy, looks on course to deputise once again.

Cambuur possible starting lineup:.

Jansen; Bouah, Baouf, Van Duijl, Costarelli; Souren, Maertens; Ceka, Arguioui, Hamache; Binder.

Sparta Rotterdam possible starting lineup:.

Bednarek; Kuipers, Vianello, Young, Martes; Hatenboer, Baas; Van Bergen, Mito, Babadi; Zonneveld.

Cambuur’s recent form gives them confidence, and despite their poor record in this fixture, they remain favourites to claim victory.

We are tipping the home side to carry the day when all is mentioned and done.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham head coach Scott Parker has refused to commit to either Mads Hermansen or Fin Herrick ahead of Saturday’s Championship clash against Stoke City. The Hammers boss was asked about his goalkeeping selection during today’s pre-match press conference and was decidedly non-committal.

Speaking to the club’s official website, Parker mentioned: “I’ve been hugely impressed with both Mads [Hermansen] and Fin [Herrick], so we’ll manage things, keep working hard and then make our decision.”.

According to recent reports, “As always, we’ll see. The goalkeeping position is probably one of the hardest on the pitch. You’re there for all eyes to see.”.

Personally, I would start with Mads Hermansen in goal against Stoke City. I completely understand why Scott Parker chose to go with Fin Herrick over the last couple of games, but the truth is it hasn’t worked.

I’ve little doubt that the last couple of performances will have dented the young keeper’s confidence, and taking him out of the firing line might not be a bad thing.

Hermansen, whose recent performances have seen him dropped from the West Ham team.

Unfortunately, we’re currently in a situation where it’s a case of picking whoever is the least worst, rather than selecting a player because they’ve done something impressive.

If Parker’s non-committal comments are anything to go by, I suspect we’ll see Hermansen reinstated to the team to face Stoke.

Published: 09:12 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 09:12 EST, 25 November 2026.

Conor Coady has emerged as one of the candidates to become upcoming head coach at Blackpool.

The struggling League One side are looking for a fresh manager after firing Ian Evatt on his birthday last week.

They salvaged a draw against Leicester City on Tuesday to stay just above the drop zone in 20th place with caretaker Steve Thompson in charge.

The Tangerines are understood to have been inundated with applications with the likes of Conor Hourihane, who left Leicester City as assistant manager earlier this month, Matt Bloomfield, formerly Oxford United boss, and Richie Wellens of Leyton Orient among the leading names in the frame.

However, Daily Mail Sport understands former England, Wolves and Everton defender Coady is also being considered.

Conor Coady, pictured here working as England Under-21s assistant, could take over at Blackpool.

The 33-year-old retired from playing on November 6 after stints with Wrexham and Charlton Athletic and took up a role as assistant to Lee Carsley in the England U21 set-up in September, replacing Ashley Cole.

Coady had also been helping out within his first club Liverpool's U21 set-up, prior to his deadline day departure from Wrexham.

He is keen to make the step up in club coaching and was linked with a role at Barnsley in recent weeks.

West Ham United v Stoke City EFL Championship, London Stadium, Saturday 28 November 2026, 3pm GMT.

Sources indicate that scott Parker is under massive pressure at West Ham. In most circumstances, no head coach should face any sort of scrutiny after four games, but managing the Hammers is a very nuanced challenge and he will not be given an infinite amount of time to turn this around.

For a club possessing arguably the most expensive squad in the division, and one which broke the Championship transfer record to sign Arne Engels, spiralling down the league is not acceptable. Parker has inherited plenty of problems, but he was also appointed to deliver immediate promotion.

In a recent development, A rousing 3-3 comeback at Cardiff City has been followed by defeats against Blackburn Rovers and Portsmouth, either side of a disappointing home draw with bottom club Preston North End. Parker is still searching for his first victory, while second-placed Stoke arrive at London Stadium on a five-match winning run.

Having watched Tuesday night’s game from the second row at Fratton Park, I was frightened by the lack of belief in some of our players. The 1-0 defeat against Portsmouth was not just another unlucky result in which West Ham failed to convert chances.

It has been revealed that the team looked fragile, uncertain and short of attacking inspiration. Portsmouth were able to handle us comfortably, and West Ham have now collected only two points from the last 18 available.

Parker is already under huge pressure at West Ham.

Parker noted after the game that the group needs to “fix up” and give itself a platform, while acknowledging the need to rebuild the players’ belief. That was perhaps the most worrying aspect of the defeat because this is a squad which should not require a confidence transplant before every Championship fixture.

It has been revealed that parker’s immediate job is to get West Ham to the January transfer window without becoming completely cut adrift. There is still enough time to rescue the season, but the Hammers cannot continue losing ground while waiting for injured players to return or new signings to arrive.

I would take this opportunity to make numerous changes. Parker is nowhere near discovering his first-choice XI, so there is probably little harm in experimenting because there is currently very little for him to build upon.

Both full-back positions need addressing, as do West Ham’s striking problems. If I were selecting the team, I would consider playing Arne Engels at right-back simply to try something different, with Ollie Scarles coming in on the opposite side.

According to recent reports, however, I don’t expect Parker to make too many changes. The Hammers head coach continues to speak about consistency and stability, so he is unlikely to rip everything up after only four matches.

In a recent development, joël Veltman struggled badly at Fratton Park, but Parker has very few alternatives while Kyle Walker-Peters remains injured. As Claret & Hugh highlighted following the Portsmouth defeat, Engels may be the only realistic emergency option unless Parker turns to an academy player.

It has been revealed that I suspect Veltman will keep his place, with Ezra Mayers continuing at left-back. Maximilian Kilman and Konstantinos Mavropanos should remain together in central defence.

Sources indicate that if Parker has any sense at all, he will draft Tomáš Souček back into the starting line-up. West Ham require leadership, physicality and somebody capable of attacking the penalty area, particularly while the recognised strikers continue to struggle.

According to recent reports, I also expect Parker to continue using a defensive midfielder. The only question is whether Edson Álvarez has recovered sufficiently to start again after an extremely intense week.

According to recent reports, álvarez had barely played serious football for months before returning against Preston and then starting at Portsmouth three days later. It would not surprise me if Parker rested him against Stoke before getting the Mexican ready to play regularly throughout the busy Christmas period.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, my best guess is that Álvarez will start behind Engels and Souček. Parker needs a result, and this does not feel like an obvious occasion to remove one of the few players who has improved the midfield.

Industry observers note that jarrod Bowen should continue on the right, although I would still prefer to see West Ham’s best attacking player used more centrally. Edvin Austbø is likely to retain his position on the left, with Joël Piroe starting up front largely because Parker has so few convincing alternatives.

Stoke arrive at London Stadium as the Championship’s form team, sitting second after five consecutive victories and an unbeaten run stretching to seven matches. Wednesday night’s 2-1 win over Millwall continued a sequence in which the Potters have lost only once in their last 14 league outings, so this is about as difficult as it gets for a West Ham side without a win in six.

According to recent reports, former Hammers Ben Johnson and Aaron Cresswell could both feature, with Cresswell making his first appearance of the season as a late substitute against Millwall. Djibril Soumaré and Lamine Cissé are fitness doubts, while Luca Bombino is available again after completing his one-match suspension.

Stoke travel to London Stadium as the most in-form team in the Championship, having won five consecutive matches and gone unbeaten in seven. They have lost just once in their last 14 league outings and at the moment sit second in the table.

Former Hammer Ben Johnson will also arrive with a point to prove, while Aaron Cresswell could feature after making his first appearance of the season during Wednesday’s 2-1 victory over Millwall. West Ham’s official team news confirms that Walker-Peters and Alphonse Areola are still being assessed.

Considering West Ham could not beat the division’s bottom club and were then comfortably handled by Portsmouth, I’m struggling to find any convincing reason to predict victory against the Championship’s best-performing side.

I hope I’m wrong, but nothing I have seen from Parker’s West Ham suggests we are ready to beat Stoke.

West Ham United 0-2 Stoke City.

Industry observers note that "I think I felt the love. I'm not just saying it. I really have, and that's why I want to stay here and continue playing.

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 10:26 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 10:37 EST, 25 November 2026.

James Penrice has warned that Rangers can forget about going top of the table on Saturday if they play like they did for the first 45 minutes against Aberdeen.

Derek McInnes’ side were a goal down at half-time and heading to their first defeat in 14 games after failing to get going against the Dons.

With the manager making three changes at half-time, the Ibrox men scored three times in an incredible 11-minute burst through Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin.

And while Aberdeen netted again via Findlay Marshall, Rangers hung on for the win which put them within a point of Celtic.

Industry observers note that with the leaders facing Hearts at Tynecastle on Sunday, McInnes’ men can move to the summit if they defeat high-flying Falkirk the day before. But Penrice notes that will only happen if they deliver a more complete display than they showed on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that ‘It’s a massive incentive for us, but the league isn’t won in November,’ noted the defender. ‘Falkirk are playing well. They’ve travelled well away from home too.

James Penrice has warned Rangers they will need to improve if they are to take top spot.

It has been revealed that ‘We’ll need to be on it. We can’t go into that game like we did on Tuesday night. I wouldn’t say we were lucky, but we can’t concede two goals at home. We can’t do that on Saturday.

‘Is it vital we grab that chance (to go top)? Definitely. We’ll just concentrate on ourselves. It’s another game to tick off and we’ll turn up hoping to get the three points.’.

McInnes introduced Tuur Rommens, Findlay Curtis and Kim Min-su at the break with the changes leading to a much-improved display.

Despite chalking up the win which maintained the unbeaten run, Penrice insists the overall show left considerable room for improvement.

Industry observers note that ‘It was very mixed,’ he reflected. ‘We concede in the first half, but then fly out the traps in the second.

‘I thought we were really good for 20 minutes. We go and score a third and look comfortable. But then we switch off. We turned our back at a free-kick and they end up scoring. We made it difficult for ourselves.

Sources indicate that ‘But we got three goals. Ryan got his usual one where he’s alive in the box. Gas was brilliant and he got his goal then Nico got his. But again, we made it hard for ourselves. The main thing is we got three points.

In a recent development, ‘We made a few changes at half-time and I thought the boys who came on were brilliant. They had that real spark and energy. We started the second half really well but, ultimately, we need to score more.

Rangers goalscorers Djeidi Gassama, Nico Raskin and Ryan Naderi celebrate against Aberdeen.

‘We could have done that and made it easy for ourselves.’.

According to recent reports, rangers haven’t now tasted defeat since losing away to Czech side Jablonec on August 27. And while not every display in that run has been outstanding, Penrice is encouraged by the fact that the team is showing plenty of character.

‘We’ve shown we’ve got a bit of resilience,’ he remarked. ‘It’s not a bad trait to be winning games and scoring late on. We’re doing that. But as players we want to make the game as easy as possible.

‘We’re on a run just now and hopefully it continues.

‘The positives on Tuesday night were that, in spells, we were really good. We were flying in the second half. But we can’t concede two goals at home and expect to always come away with a win.’.

Meanwhile, Penrice indicates he’s got no fears that Min-su will become a goal threat for the team.

The South Korean, an £8.5million summer signing from Girona, has yet to find the net in 14 appearances with his sole assist coming against Motherwell last Saturday.

The forward thought he’d broken his duck with a spectacular late effort against the Dons only for the ball to sail over.

‘I remarked to Min-su at full-time that me and massive Ryan were ready to run to him at 100mph if he’d scored that goal,’ Penrice smiled.

In a recent development, ‘You can see he wants it so bad. He probably just needs to calm down in front of goal.

‘I thought that was the one when he chopped inside. I thought he was scoring, but he put it into row Z.

Kim Min-su has impressed for Rangers but is still waiting to score his first goal for the club.

‘It wasn’t ideal, but he was still happy afterward because we won the game.

According to recent reports, ‘You can see in his game that, at every opportunity, he’s trying to get a shot away. It will come and hopefully it comes at a perfect time.

‘There’s a reason these players are at Ibrox — it’s because they’re extremely talented. It’s just that last bit but they’re very young.

Sources indicate that ‘Min-su’s game isn’t just goals and assists. He’s a really talented footballer who creates problems for teams. He’s been a massive part of why we’re on this run. You can all see it.

‘It’s about more than goals and assists, but if he adds that to his game, he’s only going to go on and have a very successful career.

According to recent reports, ‘That’s what the boys want for him. We want our wide players and strikers to score as many as possible.’.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while Mads Hermansen’s recent performances have come under scrutiny and Finlay Herrick has found the transition challenging, culminating in his role in Portsmouth’s winning goal on Tuesday night, I still believe Herrick has the attributes to succeed.
  • Meanwhile, supporters continue to ask why Alphonse Areola has not been available for first-team selection.
  • Last season, the French goalkeeper conceded 37 goals in 20 Premier League appearances, made 77 saves and failed to keep a single clean sheet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while Mads Hermansen’s recent performances have come under scrutiny and Finlay Herrick has found the transition challenging, culminating in his role in Portsmouth’s winning goal on Tuesday night, I still believe Herrick has the attributes to succeed. His potential is clear, but it requires time, guidance and development.

Meanwhile, supporters continue to ask why Alphonse Areola has not been available for first-team selection.

Let’s start with the facts. Alphonse Areola is no messiah. Last season, the French goalkeeper conceded 37 goals in 20 Premier League appearances, made 77 saves and failed to keep a single clean sheet. At the start of this season, Areola was informed that he was no longer Nuno’s first-choice goalkeeper. Despite having just one year remaining on his contract and reportedly taking a 50 per cent reduction in salary, now believed to be around £60,000 per week, no offers materialised. That still makes him one of the highest-paid goalkeepers in the Championship.

Sources indicate that this season, he has been named on the bench nine times in 17 matches. However, questions remain over his fitness. Earlier in the campaign, he was sidelined with an unspecified injury despite being photographed attending a tennis tournament. He then reportedly suffered another setback during the warm-up ahead of the Blackburn Rovers match on 7 November, although the club has yet to officially disclose the nature of the injury.

Industry observers note that scott Parker has offered little clarity, saying only that “the club was struggling a bit with Alphonse” and describing his availability as “touch and go”. Inevitably, conspiracy theories have emerged, with some suggesting the goalkeeper has chosen not to make himself available for selection. However, there is no evidence to substantiate that suggestion, and he attended the Preston game with his family and watched from the stands.

The most likely explanation, as Martin previously outlined, is simply fitness, or a lack of it. For a club with only two recognised senior goalkeepers and one established academy option, the current situation is far from ideal.

It has been revealed that while the team’s defensive issues cannot be blamed solely on the goalkeeping department, the number of goals conceded this season has undoubtedly affected results. It is an glitch that requires an urgent resolution and one Parker will be acutely aware of.

Recent findings suggest that another area worth examining is the goalkeeping coaching set-up. Since Xavi Valero’s departure in May 2025, the club has never truly found a settled replacement. Casper Ankergren arrived alongside Linus Kandolin, Rui Barbosa subsequently replaced them and Billy Lepine later stepped into the role. In the space of just 18 months, the club has had four different goalkeeping coaches.

Continuity matters, particularly in such a specialised position, and that level of turnover is far from ideal.

For me, the club already has a ready-made solution in Łukasz Fabiański. His experience, leadership and understanding of the position make him more than qualified to take on such a responsibility.

Whatever the answer, Parker needs to resolve the situation swiftly. The clock is ticking.

Ipswich Town vs Aston Villa - prediction, team news, lineups

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Oliver Thomas | 26 Nov 2026 19:00, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 18:48.
  • Aston Villa travel to Portman Road to face Ipswich Town on Saturday evening seeking to climb back into the top half of the Premier League table.
  • Both meetings between these two sides during the 2024-25 season ended in entertaining draws (2-2 in Suffolk and 1-1 at Villa Park), leaving the Tractor Boys still searching for their first top-flight triumph over the Lions since February 1993.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Oliver Thomas | 26 Nov 2026 19:00, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 18:48.

Aston Villa travel to Portman Road to face Ipswich Town on Saturday evening seeking to climb back into the top half of the Premier League table.

Both meetings between these two sides during the 2024-25 season ended in entertaining draws (2-2 in Suffolk and 1-1 at Villa Park), leaving the Tractor Boys still searching for their first top-flight triumph over the Lions since February 1993.

Tipped by many to struggle before the season began, Ipswich are yet to spend a single day sitting in the Premier League relegation zone since securing promotion, but their recent form has seen them slip closer to the bottom three.

After winning three of their first six top-flight games this term (L3), the Tractor Boys have failed to come out on top in any of their last five fixtures (D2 L3), suffering defeats to Bournemouth (2-1) and Tottenham (2-0) either side of the international break.

Gary O'Neil acknowledged that his team “didn't get to our level enough” against Spurs and they now sit down in 16th place in the table, just two points above the drop zone with games against Villa, Coventry City, Leeds United, Newcastle United and Brighton & Hove Albion up next.

Another “soft” goal was conceded by Ipswich last time out, and they have now shipped a total of 22 goals in 11 Premier League matches – the third-most in the division – while they have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their last 30 top-flight games; only West Brom between August 2010 and May 2011 have endured a longer run in the division’s history (34 games).

Ipswich have also proved largely incapable of mounting second-half comebacks, failing to win any of the 22 Premier League matches in which they have trailed at half time since the start of the 2024-25 season (D3 L19). Striking first on Saturday could therefore be crucial for O'Neil’s side as they bid to upset Villa.

Since securing a 2-1 home victory over Man City on October 24, Aston Villa have failed to win any of their last six matches in all competitions (D3 L3), suffering a narrow 1-0 defeat at Galatasaray in the Champions League on Tuesday.

Unai Emery’s side previously played out a frustrating goalless stalemate at home to Sunderland in the Premier League, their third top-flight draw in a row that leaves them sitting 12th in the table and seven points behind fourth spot where they finished last season.

Villa – who have not drawn four consecutive Premier League matches since September 2011 – are preparing for a historic milestone on Saturday, as they play their 5,000th match across the top-four tiers of English football (W2,050 D1,199 L1,750), becoming the 16th club to reach the landmark.

Emery is keen to see his team rediscover their clinical touch in front of goal sooner rather than later, as Villa have failed to score in four of their last six games, not registering a single shot on target against Galatasaray.

Heading into Saturday’s clash in Suffolk, Villa have not lost any of their last 10 visits to Ipswich (D6 L3) in all competitions (W5 D4) since a 1-0 EFL Cup loss back in December 1992, while they are unbeaten in all 22 of their league matches against promoted sides under Emery (W15 D7).

Aston Villa Premier League form:.

Ipswich boss O'Neil has confirmed that Leif Davis has recovered from a knock to his ankle sustained in the defeat at Spurs, and the left-back will start this weekend.

Darnell Furlong started at right-back last time out, but O'Neil may be tempted to select either Abdoul Ouattara or Dara O'Shea on the right side of a four-man defence.

Zian Flemming was handed his first league start for Ipswich last time out, but he could be replaced up front by Emersonn, while Abdul Fatawu, Florentino Luis, Jack Clarke and Jacob Greaves will also be pushing to start after beginning as substitutes last weekend.

As for Aston Villa, Amadou Onana (knee) and Matteo Ruggeri (hamstring) remain sidelined through injury, but Matty Cash is available for selection after serving concussion protocols.

Cash is therefore expected to replace Taylor Harwood-Bellis and start at right-back, while Pau Torres is set to be recalled at centre-back at the expense of former Ipswich man Tyrone Mings.

With Alejandro Garnacho facing an uncertain future at Villa, Emery is likely to favour Alysson and Johan Manzambi in wide positions, providing support in attack for striker Nicolas Jackson who has netted six goals in 10 Premier League games this season.

Ipswich Town possible starting lineup:.

Walton; O'Shea, Diop, Greaves, Davis; Lukic, Palacios; Clarke, Enciso, Maeda; Emersonn.

Aston Villa possible starting lineup:.

Suzuki; Cash, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Kamara, Goretzka; Alysson, McGinn, Manzambi; Jackson.

While Portman Road remains a far more forgiving environment for O'Neil’s side, who have collected seven of their 11 points on home soil this term (W2 D1 L2), Villa should relish the opportunity to rediscover their scoring touch against a porous Ipswich defence shipping an average of two goals per game.

Although the Tractor Boys are capable of keeping things competitive in Suffolk, we are backing Emery’s men to shake off their recent slump and grind out a hard-fought victory.

Recent findings suggest that west Ham United have received a timely boost ahead of Saturday’s Championship clash against Stoke City, with Tomáš Souček back in training at Rush Green. The Czech midfielder suffered a nasty cut near his left eye during Tuesday night’s defeat at Portsmouth but is hoping to be involved against the Potters.

Sources indicate that speaking to the club’s official website this morning, Souček revealed that he was feeling good despite requiring stitches and expects to wear a bandage if he plays tomorrow. The 31-year-old also highlighted the importance of matching the opposition’s intensity when West Ham are without the ball. Having impressed during his substitute appearance at Fratton Park, Souček has certainly made a strong case for a return to the starting line-up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Liverpool have been dealt a fresh injury concern in the first half of their Champions League fixture against Club Brugge on Wednesday night.

The Reds got off to a strong start at the Jan Breydel Stadium as they pounced on a loose pass by Yann Sommer to take the lead through a close-range finish from Alexander Isak.

However, Andoni Iraola was left wincing in the technical area when, shortly before half-time, Victor Munoz went to ground and stayed there after a surging run into the hosts’ penalty area was abruptly halted.

It swiftly became clear that the Liverpool winger was in pain, and a stretcher was readied before the Spaniard got to his feet and was able to limp off, with Rio Ngumoha coming on in his place (Sky Sports).

(Photo by Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images).

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

The sight of Munoz standing up and walking (gingerly) off the pitch came as a relief, but to lose the 23-year-old in such innocuous circumstances represents a big body blow to Liverpool.

The summer signing from Osasuna has had to rely mostly on substitute appearances so far in his Reds career, but he was handed a start by Iraola tonight off the back of his fine showing off the bench against Manchester United on Sunday.

The Spanish winger rounded off the scoring in that match and had Club Brugge terrified with some mazy, proactive dribbling before that unfortunate injury setback when he overstretched to try and get to the ball.

It remains to be seen just how seriously Munoz has been hurt and whether he’ll face a lengthy spell on the sidelines, but we can only keep our fingers crossed that it isn’t as bad as what it initially seemed.

Iraola might be able to provide us with an upgrade after full-time, even if it’d only be a preliminary indication.

#165336. Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

📅 28 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 80m • 📚 Deep Dive (15910 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

📅 28 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 80 min read (15910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~80 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2.
  • Industry observers note that although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7.
  • By contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics1,2. Although the landscape of height-associated common genetic variation has been studied extensively2, rare variation remains relatively unexplored1. Here, using rare protein-altering variants in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes, we identify 207 height-associated genes, 98% of which replicate in an additional 624,567 individuals. The rarest and most deleterious class of variation, singleton (frequency < 0.0001%) putative loss-of-function variants, implicated 17 genes with large effects on height ranging from −17cm (ACAN) to +11 cm (FBN1) per allele, 52× larger than the average effect of common height-associated variants and comparable to the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score. Several genes (TET1, DTL and IGF2BP2) have effect sizes that are at least as large as established Mendelian height genes, yet lack documented stature or skeletal growth syndromes, particularly for genes associated with increased height. Our large-scale sequencing study elucidates the genetic architecture and allelic heterogeneity of rare variants in height, providing unique insights into their large effects—often similar to or larger than recognized Mendelian syndromes—and their impact on trait prediction, clinical evaluation, and discovery power to facilitate drug target prioritization.

Industry observers note that although height was described as a heritable trait as early as 18863, its genetic architecture started to emerge only in the late twentieth century when researchers began identifying the genetic causes of Mendelian syndromes with a substantial stature component4,5,6,7. Non-syndromic genetic modulators of height remained unclear until 2007, when genome-wide association studies (GWASs) identified the first common variants associated with height8. Fifteen years later, a GWAS of 5.3 million individuals identified 12,111 independent variants that collectively accounted for 40% of the variance in height across individuals of European descent2. As with other traits, height GWASs predominantly implicated common non-coding variants with modest effects (<1 cm)2, complicating efforts to link associations directly to specific genes and functional mechanisms.

By contrast, sequencing-based studies of rare variation can directly implicate causal genes by identifying large-effect putative loss-of-function (pLoF) and missense variants9. To systematically assess the contribution of rare coding variation to height, we performed a multiancestry exome sequencing analysis of adult height in 1,450,633 individuals across 12 cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), in which we (1) identified 17 height-associated genes through a burden of singleton pLoFs; (2) identified additional height-associated genes by including nonsynonymous variants up to 1% alternate allele frequency (AAF) and applying non-burden tests that do not assume variant effects act in the same direction; and (3) estimated the impact of rare protein-altering variation on genetic-based height prediction.

In a recent development, using 826,066 individuals from six cohorts (Supplementary Table 1), we performed three discovery association analyses of adult height: (1) imputed common variants (AAF > 0.01); (2) rare exome variants (AAF ≤ 0.01, alternate allele count (AAC) ≥ 10); and (3) gene-based tests grouping rare coding variants. We used a single unified Bonferroni significance threshold of 1.75 × 10−9 across all three analyses (Methods). For gene-based analyses, we used a gene-wide omnibus statistic, gene-P10, that aggregates evidence across burden tests and two other gene-based tests, variant-level aggregate Cauchy association tests (ACAT-V)11 and optimal sequence kernel association tests (SKAT-O)12 (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1). We used six additional cohorts with 624,567 individuals for replication (Supplementary Table 1) and assessed the impact of rare variants on height prediction using a subset (n = 242,679).

Sources indicate that common variant analysis identified 3,034 conditionally independent height associations (Supplementary Table 2) that collectively explain around 25% of the observed variation in height (Methods and Supplementary Note). We conditioned on these 3,034 common variants to ensure rare variant and gene-based associations were independent of common variant signals (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Fig. 2). We identified 105 rare nonsynonymous variants in 87 genes (median AAF = 2.16 × 10−3; Supplementary Table 3) and 207 genes associated with height (gene-P < 1.75 × 10−9; Extended Data Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 4). In total, 82 out of the 87 genes with significant rare nonsynonymous variant associations are also among the 207 genes identified through gene-based tests.

As singleton pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of variants, we first focused on this subset. Singleton pLoF burden tests identified 17 genes, 11 height decreasing and 6 height increasing, with a mean absolute effect of 8.92 cm per allele (Fig. 1, Table 1 and Supplementary Tables 5 and 6), about 52× larger than the average GWAS variant (\(\overline{|{\beta }_{\mathrm{GWAS}}|}\) = 0.17 cm) and around 44× larger (range 14.4× to 78.3×) when comparing effects per gene (Methods and Supplementary Table 7). Effects ranged from a 16.6-cm decrease in stature for ACAN singleton pLoF carriers to an 11.1-cm increase in stature for FBN1 singleton pLoF carriers. The effect of carrying a singleton pLoF in one of these 17 genes approaches the cumulative effect observed in the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score (PGS) (top 1%, +9.60 cm; bottom 1%, −9.12 cm; Fig. 2a, Methods and Supplementary Tables 8 and 9). These incredibly rare pLoFs, cumulatively carried by fewer than 0.1% of individuals (744 carriers among 826,066 individuals), have a larger impact on height than all but the most extreme combinations of common variants.

a, pLoF burden effect sizes across AAFs for 17 genes identified by a significant burden of singleton pLoFs (Table 1). b, Same genes as in a, with effect sizes from singleton burden tests across variant classes displayed. c, The relationship between AAF, variant class, effect size, and discovery yield for 179 genes identified from burden tests (Supplementary Tables 6 and 10). Inside each point is the number of genes discovered (top) and the absolute mean effect (in centimetres; bottom). Effect sizes were estimated by multiplying β by the s.d. of observed height (about 7.99 cm). All P values are two-sided, calculated by REGENIE in discovery analysis (n = 826,066), and significance assessed using a P-value threshold of 1.75 × 10−9.

a, Percentiles of a height PGS (grey) derived from common variants (AAF > 1%; 3,034 GWAS variants + 5 common exome variants; Supplementary Table 8) representing the mean height difference between replication individuals in each PGS percentile (n = 2,427) compared with the remaining ancestry/sex-matched individuals (n = 240,252; Supplementary Table 9). The coloured points are mean significant burden test effect sizes (split by effect direction) placed for comparison to the PGS. The error bars represent 95% CIs around the mean effect estimated from REGENIE. b, The inverse relationship between effect size (in centimetres; y axis) and AAF (x axis) for burden tests (Supplementary Table 6), exome variants (Supplementary Table 3) and conditionally independent common variants (Supplementary Table 2) from discovery (n = 826,066 individuals). The triangles denote burden tests (with a smaller shape for the burden AAF threshold embedded inside), and the circles denote individual variants. The colour denotes the predicted consequence of individual variants or variants included in the burden test. The full distribution is shown in the inset.

These 17 genes belong to well-established biological processes and pathways affecting height, including extracellular matrix organization and skeletal/growth pathways such as growth hormone/insulin-like growth factor (GH/IGF), WNT/β-catenin and transforming growth factor-β1,13,14,15 (TGFβ) (Table 1 and Extended Data Table 1).

Incorporating more common variation into burden tests can increase statistical power for gene discovery by adding variant carriers, although at the cost of attenuated effect sizes. Expanding our analysis to include increasingly frequent pLoFs, followed by including missense variants, identified an additional 162 genes (Extended Data Fig. 1).

Industry observers note that among pLoFs, relaxing the burden test AAF threshold from singletons (about 0.00006%) to 1% identified 76 genes, 62 not discovered with pLoF singletons alone. On average, burden tests aggregating more common pLoFs had a 3.96-cm effect—less than half the 8.92-cm effect of pLoF singletons, but still 24× larger than the average GWAS association (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Among the 15 genes with pLoF singleton associations that remained significant at AAF < 0.01%, we observed a 35% attenuation in the absolute effect size (from 8.71 cm to 5.68 cm), suggesting that a substantial fraction of more frequent pLoF-annotated variants may not cause complete loss of function. Two genes—CHD8 (associated with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability) and COL1A1 (associated with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome16 and osteogenesis imperfecta)—were identified only through singleton pLoF burden tests. When more frequent pLoFs were included, burden test effect sizes fell by 78% for COL1A1 and 83% for CHD8 and were no longer statistically significant (Fig. 1a). By contrast, three genes with absolute effects on height of >1 s.d. (7.99 cm) reached significance only with higher-frequency pLoFs: SHOX17 in the fibroblast growth factor pathway (β = −12.05 cm, P = 2.85 × 10−16); transcriptional regulator ERF (β = −8.67 cm, P = 4.41 × 10−21); and HMGA2, the insulin-like growth factor pathway gene underlying the first height GWAS discovery8 (β = −8.11 cm, P = 6.11 × 10−13). These three genes each had few singleton pLoFs (1, 6, and 16 carriers, respectively); aggregating singletons with additional rare pLoFs was therefore essential to achieve significance.

This expanded set of height-associated pLoF burden genes highlighted additional canonical growth pathways and height biology (for example, the fibroblast growth factor pathway; Extended Data Table 1), as well as additional members from the same gene families and pathways implicated by pLoF singleton genes (Supplementary Table 11).

Whereas pLoFs represent the rarest and most deleterious class of coding variation, missense variants represent the most frequent class of protein-altering variants9,18,19. If missense variants ablate protein function to a similar extent as pLoFs, we might expect both increased statistical power and similar effect sizes when combining both in burden tests. Conversely, if missense variants only partially diminish protein function or exert opposing effects through gain-of-function (GoF) mechanisms, burden effect sizes will be attenuated.

We combined pLoFs with three sets of missense variants: (1) all missense variants; (2) missense variants inconsistently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (possibly deleterious); and (3) missense variants confidently classified as deleterious by in silico algorithms (deleterious; Methods), collectively identifying 154 genes (85 not discovered by pLoFs alone; Fig. 1c). When combined with pLoF variants, successively filtering rare missense variants for increasing deleteriousness increased discovery power, yielding 96, 116, and 132 genes for each of the above groups, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Among the 14 genes with both significant singleton pLoF and singleton pLoF + deleterious missense burden associations (Table 1), the absolute effect size decreased 28.5% on average when adding deleterious missense singletons (8.70 cm versus 6.22 cm; Fig. 1b). This observation holds broadly across height-associated genes, with diminished pLoF + missense effect sizes reflecting both that missense variants account for most rare allele carriers (68.5% in singleton and 84.1% in AAF < 1% burden tests) and that the effect of missense variants is, on average, substantially smaller than that of pLoFs (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Table 10). Despite diminished effect sizes, the higher allele counts contributed by missense variants substantially increased overall discovery power, more than doubling the number of associated height genes.

Of the 85 genes not discovered by pLoFs alone, UHRF2 (singleton pLoF + deleterious missense variants: β = −4.74 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−12)—an E3 ubiquitin ligase regulating the cell cycle20—and PTPN11 (pLoF + deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.01%: β = −4.00 cm, P = 2.5 × 10−32)—a signalling protein involved in development and hormone response through the RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT signalling pathways21—had the largest effect sizes.

It has been revealed that we found six genes (ESR1, FGFR3, HSD11B2, MTMR11, PTPN11 and RPL5) that exhibited the strongest association from missense-only burden tests, and pLoF burden tests were, at best, only nominally significant (Supplementary Table 13). Four genes (FGFR3, HSD11B2, PTPN11 and RPL5) had opposite directions of effect between pLoF and missense burden tests, although the pLoF estimates were not statistically significant. Notably, three genes—FGFR3 (refs. 7,22), PTPN11 (ref. 23) and ESR1 (ref. 24)—have previously reported GoF mutations that drive syndromic conditions with notable skeletal growth phenotypes, including achondroplasia (FGFR3)22 and Noonan syndrome (PTPN11)23. Given the known GoF mechanisms for three of these genes, the other missense-driven genes may also affect height through GoF mechanisms.

The new genes identified by incorporating missense variants further underscore previously implicated pathways, biological functions and gene families (Supplementary Table 11) but also implicate different pathways (for example, Sonic Hedgehog signalling) and biological processes, including sex hormone regulation and carbohydrate transport, storage and metabolism (Extended Data Table 1).

Although burden tests identified 179 height-associated genes (Extended Data Fig. 1a), they were not designed to identify genes of which variants with effects exist in opposite directions or where most variants have no effect. For these situations, SKAT-O12 and ACAT-V11 were developed.

Collectively, ACAT-V and SKAT-O identified 28 genes not detected by burden tests (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Before conditional analysis, ACAT-V and SKAT-O associations were more likely than burden test associations to be driven by linkage disequilibrium with common variants (Supplementary Note, Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 12). Consistent with the underlying model, SKAT-O associations highlight genes harbouring variants with opposing effects on height. For example, in PTCH1, a transmembrane protein receptor involved in Hedgehog signalling25, the SKAT-O association (P = 1.94 × 10−15) was driven by two variants: a missense variant associated with increased height (9:95458026G>A; p.T1052M; β = +1.00 cm, P = 4.8 × 10−11; Supplementary Table 3) and a splice acceptor variant associated with decreased height (9:95485875C>T; β = −4.28 cm, P = 1.9 × 10−9). Meanwhile, ACAT-V identified genes like FBN2 (P = 1.72 × 10−12), a component of microfibrils that stores and regulates growth factors including TGFβ26, in which the association was driven by one significant missense variant (5:128332993G>T; p.H1381N; β = +1.07 cm, P = 9.8 × 10−14; AAF = 0.48%; Supplementary Table 3).

Although gene-based tests are useful for boosting rare variant discovery power, we identified 121 significant rare (AAF < 1%) exome variants after conditioning on common GWAS variants (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Tables 3 and 14 and Supplementary Note). Of these 121 variants, 105 were nonsynonymous (85 missense, 17 pLoFs and 3 in-frame insertions or deletions (indels)) and implicated 87 genes, 82 of which overlapped genes implicated by gene-based tests (60 from burden tests; 22 genes from ACAT-V or SKAT-O).

It has been revealed that for the 82 genes identified by both single variants and gene-based tests, we compared the consistency of effect sizes between burden test and significant individual variants (Methods). Focusing on the 79 rare nonsynonymous variants (59 missense, 17 pLoFs, 3 in-frame indels) in 60 genes with a significant burden test, we found that 52 (66%) had larger effect sizes than the largest burden test effect. The neurodevelopmental-disorder-associated gene KMT2B27 had the largest discrepancy, with a nearly 20-fold difference between variant 19:35720959C>T (p.R538C; β = −7.67 cm, P = 2.6 × 10−10, AAF = 2.61 × 10−5) and the largest burden test effect (β = −0.38 cm, P = 5.0×10−10; pLoF and possibly deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.01%).

According to recent reports, two genes with GoF missense variants, FGFR3 and PTPN11, have multiple missense variants with some of the largest observed effects on height (Fig. 2b). Among the six exome-wide significant variants in FGFR3, a pathogenic GoF missense variant causing achondroplasia7 (4:1804392G>A; p.G380R; P = 3.22 × 10−64) decreases height by 29.78 cm, about 13× larger than the largest FGFR3 burden test effect (β = −2.31 cm, P = 2 × 10−41; deleterious missense variants AAF < 0.0001; Extended Data Fig. 2). PTPN11 also contains two significant pathogenic GoF missense variants23,28: p.R265Q (12:112472981G>A; β = −12.26 cm, P = 6 × 10−19) and p.N308D (12:112477719A>G; β = −14.21 cm, P = 4 × 10−14), with effects around 3× larger than the largest burden signal (β = −4.12 cm, P = 3.6 × 10−33; deleterious missense variants with AAF < 0.0001). These examples emphasize the challenge that allelic heterogeneity presents for interpreting and using gene-level burden effect sizes. We discuss the implications of effect size heterogeneity on phenotypic prediction below (see the ‘Heritability, enrichment and prediction’ section).

Recent studies29,30 demonstrated that non-additive models can identify associations missed by standard approaches; we therefore tested rare coding variants under a recessive model. This identified only one association missed by additive tests: the CFTR ΔF508 mutation that causes cystic fibrosis31 was not associated with height under an additive model (βadd = −0.05 cm; Padd = 0.14), but was associated with a 5.87-cm height reduction in homozygotes in the recessive model (Prec = 5 × 10−10; replication and additional details are provided in the Supplementary Note). This result is consistent with both the recessive nature of cystic fibrosis mutations and the established impact of cystic fibrosis on growth and stature. The inability of cystic fibrosis treatments to fully restore growth trajectory and stature, along with diminished IGF1 levels exhibited by newborns with cystic fibrosis, are findings compatible with a direct effect of CFTR on height through fetal and/or neonatal growth pathways32,33.

Recent findings suggest that we sought to understand the differences in genetic architecture across genetic ancestry groups by stratifying single-variant and gene-based tests by ancestry (Methods). Consistent with previous findings, we detected no effect-size heterogeneity by genetic ancestry34. However, we identified several ancestry-specific signals resulting from differences in AAF and sample size. Most associations specific to a single ancestry were identified in the European subset, which accounts for most participants (n = 640,240, 78%; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). One notable exception is a rare HHIP p.V496E substitution associated with decreased height exclusively in the admixed American subpopulation (AMR AAF = 0.05%, P = 1.52 × 10−9, β = −3.96 cm; Supplementary Table 15 and Supplementary Note). This variant is observed only in individuals from the Mexico City Prospective Study35. We speculate that the p.V496E variant is a GoF missense variant, as rare HHIP pLoFs appear to be associated with increased height (pLoF singleton β = +9.92 cm, P = 3.72 × 10−7). Similarly, we replicate a known signal at a FBN1 missense variant36 (p.E1297G; β = −2.12 cm, P = 2.9 × 10−17; Supplementary Table 16) that is substantially more common in admixed Americans (about 1% versus 0.004% in Europeans) and occurs almost exclusively on Indigenous haplotypes (Supplementary Fig. 4). These discoveries underscore the value of sequencing diverse populations.

Height GWASs14 have consistently observed enrichment of Mendelian syndrome genes among height-associated common variant loci37; we observed similar enrichment in genes implicated through rare variation. Forty-three out of 76 genes (57%) with significant pLoF burden signals at AAF < 1% and 102 out of 207 (49%) height-associated genes in total were documented in the Mendelian syndrome in Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, significantly more than expected by chance (odds ratio (OR) = 4.46, 95% confidence interval (CI) = 2.76–7.26, P = 1.83 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Of the 43 Mendelian genes, 21 had annotated stature or skeletal growth features2, an 8.37-fold enrichment (95% CI = 4.34–16.10, P = 2.56 × 10−10; Fisher’s exact test). Genes with pLoF burden height associations and a Mendelian syndrome listed in OMIM are over 5× more likely to be associated with decreased height (36 out of 43, 83%). Among the 11 pLoF singleton genes with height-decreasing effects, 9 were in OMIM and 8 list stature or skeletal growth among the clinical characteristics. By contrast, among the six with height-increasing effects, three are in OMIM, but only FBN1 includes height among the clinical characteristics. Our results were insufficient to determine whether increased height is under-reported as a syndromic feature or whether genes leading to increased height are less likely to cause other clinical features and therefore cause fewer recognized syndromes (Supplementary Note).

According to recent reports, previous studies estimated that the gene nearest to a GWAS peak is the causal gene in around 70% of instances9,38. We observed strong overlap between large-effect rare variant burden associations and GWAS peaks, although this overlap diminishes noticeably with the stringency of the burden definition and variant frequency. Of pLoF singleton genes, 82% (14 out of 17) are the closest gene to a GWAS peak, compared with only 60% (92 out of 154) of pLoF + missense burden genes. In total, 28 out of 207 genes are not among the top 10 nearest genes to any common variant signal. Notably, 4 genes are >1 Mb from the nearest common variant association signal: FIBIN, HHIPL1, PTPN11 and WLS. Even compared with the 12,111 index variants from ref. 2, PTPN11 is not among the 10 nearest genes to any GWAS peak, with the closest signal 393 kb away (Supplementary Table 4).

In a recent development, to assess the validity of our results, we performed replication analyses in six independent cohorts comprising an additional 624,567 individuals (Supplementary Table 1). Despite the 24.4% smaller sample size, 203 out of 207 (98.1%) genes and 113 out of 125 (90.4%) single variants replicated with nominal significance (α = 0.05; Methods, Supplementary Fig. 5, Supplementary Tables 3 and 4 and Supplementary Note), demonstrating both high consistency of height associations and the robustness of our Bonferroni threshold. Furthermore, replication rates were consistent across gene-based tests—BURDEN-ACAT, 98.1% (155 out of 158); SBAT, 93.8% (166 out of 177); SKAT-O, 95.3% (164 out of 172); and ACAT-V, 94.9% (94 out of 99; Supplementary Fig. 5b–e). Replication performance for single variants improved to 96.1% (98 out of 102) after restricting to variants with over 80% estimated replication power (Supplementary Fig. 5f). Irrespective of power, all 179 burden genes and all but one variant had consistent directions of effect between discovery and replication analyses (Supplementary Note). Furthermore, gene-based tests maintained high replication rates well above our study-wide P-value threshold (Supplementary Note and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). For example, 91.6% of the 368 genes reaching a discovery gene-P < 2.5 × 10−6—roughly equivalent to one test per gene—replicated with nominal significance (P < 0.05) and would implicate an additional 137 genes compared to our experiment-wide Bonferroni threshold (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Replication rates for single variants and singleton burden tests declined similarly, requiring respective P-value thresholds of 4 × 10−6 and 1 × 10−6 to achieve a comparable 91.6% replication rate when restricted to tests with over 80% power (Supplementary Figs. 5f and 6).

Finally, because burden tests were more likely to have negative (height-decreasing) effect estimates, we compared the ratio of effect directions across significance thresholds (Supplementary Note and Extended Data Fig. 3). The excess of height-decreasing burden effects persists well below the Bonferroni significance threshold, with the degree of imbalance varying by both significance threshold and variant class. These patterns suggest considerable rare variant signal yet to be discovered.

It has been revealed that rare variants are frequently offered as an answer to the ‘missing heritability’ problem in complex trait genetics39. Here we estimated the cumulative impact of rare coding variation on height at the population level by calculating the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to burdens of rare coding variants and assessing the potential of large-effect height-associated coding variants to improve height predictions.

First, burden heritability regression40 estimated the burden of rare nonsynonymous variants explain 3.97% (95% CI = 3.77–4.17%) of phenotypic variance (Extended Data Fig. 4, Supplementary Table 17 and Supplementary Note), nearly identical to the previously published estimate of 3.82% (95% CI = 3.55–4.09%)40. pLoFs with AAF < 0.001% accounted for the largest fraction of burden heritability, consistent with the large effects we observed for these extremely rare, damaging variants. This probably underestimates the true contribution of rare coding variants because the burden approach underestimates heritability in the presence of effect size heterogeneity40. Together, the most significant burden test for each of the 179 burden genes explains around 1.1% of phenotypic variance in the replication data, nearly 30% of the total estimated contribution of the burden of rare variants to adult height (Extended Data Fig. 5).

We next tested for enrichment of rare, deleterious variants in individuals whose height was poorly predicted by common variants in our replication data (n = 242,679), as rare variants unaccounted for in common variant prediction may contribute to the discrepancy between observed and genetically predicted height41,42,43. Individuals deviating from their common variant predicted height by >2.5 s.d. (±17–20 cm) were 17.2-fold (95% CI = 9.89–28.34, P = 1.12 × 10−16, Fisher’s exact test) enriched for carrying a singleton pLoF in one of the 17 singleton pLoF genes (Fig. 3a, Methods and Supplementary Table 18). By contrast, individuals at the extreme ends of the height distribution (>2.5 s.d.) were only 4.9-fold enriched (P = 1.89 × 10−7, Fisher’s exact test; Supplementary Table 19 and Supplementary Note) for pLoF singletons in these genes, consistent with previous results42,43.

We next focused on the 337 individuals in the replication data carrying a pLoF singleton in one of the 17 genes with significant pLoF singleton burden (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 5). In these individuals, adding burden effects to a common variant prediction model (Methods) improved the R2 from 0.55 to 0.72 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Note). This brings the performance in line with common variant prediction across the entire replication sample (R2 = 0.73). Including pLoF singleton burden effects into prediction also reduced the s.d. of the error distribution by 1.55 cm, signifying more consistent predictions; however, improvement varied substantially by gene (Fig. 3c,d and Extended Data Fig. 6).

In a recent development, given the large effects of rare missense variants in FGFR3 and PTPN11 (Fig. 2b), we evaluated the performance of several rare variant-based prediction models compared with standard common variant PGS in these variant carriers (Fig. 3d and Methods). Among 29 carriers of five rare deleterious missense variants in these two genes in the replication dataset, the prediction R2 dropped slightly from 0.158 to 0.155 when adding a PGS built from deleterious missense (AAF < 1%) burden effect sizes (Supplementary Fig. 7). By contrast, the prediction R2 increased to 0.67 when adding a PGS based on individually significant rare variants. This difference in prediction performance was especially pronounced among the six carriers of FGFR3 p.G380R (4:1804392:G:A; βdiscovery = −29.8 cm, P = 3.2 × 10−64; Fig. 2b)—a ClinVar pathogenic variant reported for achondroplasia7 (Fig. 3d))—for whom height prediction improved by an average of 26.1 cm after accounting for the variant. Aggregate burden effects are largely unsuitable in prediction for genes with substantial effect size heterogeneity, such as FGFR3 and PTPN11 (Supplementary Note). Still, individual rare variants are difficult to incorporate in prediction, as variants are frequently not observed in reference samples or effects are estimated from few observations. Overall, we observe that PGSs that supplement common variants with both aggregate rare variant effects and individual rare variants with extreme effects perform best for height prediction (Supplementary Fig. 8).

It has been revealed that finally, population-based data can provide a useful orthogonal resource to aid clinical variant interpretation19. We assessed whether our association results could inform pathogenicity classification of ClinVar variants with conflicting classifications of pathogenicity (CCOPs) or variants of uncertain significance (VUSs). To maximize power for these ultrarare variants, we performed a meta-analysis of our discovery and replication data (Supplementary Tables 20 and 21 and Extended Data Fig. 7) for the 5,233 rare variants in our 207 height-associated genes that were evaluated in ClinVar for links to stature-related syndromes (Methods). In total, 39 variants were significantly associated with height, including 20 VUSs/CCOPs. Of those 20 variants, one—an ADAMTS10 splice region variant—was associated with increased height (β = +2.3 cm, P = 3.9 × 10−15), the opposite direction of ADAMTS10’s burden test effects (Supplementary Table 6). The pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) category contained more significant height-associated variants than expected by chance (P = 6 × 10−12, binomial test), as did the CCOP and benign/likely benign categories (Supplementary Table 22).

We next looked for variants absent from ClinVar with absolute effect sizes greater than 7.99 cm (1 s.d.), an effect size greater than 77% of the stature-related P/LP variants in our 207 genes (Fig. 4). At this effect size threshold, four significant variants were completely absent from ClinVar as of July 2025 (Supplementary Table 21): pLoFs in HMGA2 (p.E98*), LCORL (p.S1370Rfs*10) and ADAMTS17 (p.S971*), and a missense substitution in ZFAT (p.R762C).
