Industry observers note that to test whether this IDR could drive liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS), we expressed EpTFIIAγ–GFP in Nicotiana benthamiana leaf epidermal cells. Upon hyperosmotic stress, EpTFIIAγ maintained a homogeneous nuclear distribution and did not coalesce into condensates under either stress or non-stress conditions (Supplementary Fig. 19a). Moreover, His–EpTFIIAγ did not detectably form dynamic droplets in vitro, indicating that its relatively short IDR was insufficient to trigger LLPS (Supplementary Fig. 19b). Further evaluation of chromatin-binding dynamics through fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy indicated that EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR) exhibited markedly shallower bleach depth and accelerated recovery kinetics (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 19c–h), indicating attenuated chromatin association and higher mobility than full-length control. Stable-transgenic EpTFIIAγ(ΔIDR) expression in wheat cv. Fielder conferred no obvious improvement in drought resistance relative to wild-type (Extended Data Fig. 6k–m), indicating that the IDR is indeed indispensable for EpTFIIAγ function in the drought-stress response.

According to recent reports, to identify EpTFIIAγ-binding sites across the wheat genome, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP–seq) with transgenic plants stably expressing EpTFIIAγ–HA in the cv. Fielder (Fig. 3d). Across two replicates, 17,131 putative EpTFIIAγ-binding sites were identified, 85% of which are in intergenic regions and 15% in genic regions, including gene bodies as well as the 3-kb upstream and 300-bp downstream flanking sequences presumed to harbour the promoter and transcriptional terminator, respectively (Fig. 3e). Analysis of 2,570 genic binding sites identified 1,347 annotated genes bound by EpTFIIAγ–HA (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Table 8), and the core motif within these binding regions was enriched with a TATA-containing element (Fig. 3g). Gene Ontology analysis found that these EpTFIIAγ–HA target genes were enriched in terms related to stress responses, such as ‘transcriptional regulation’, ‘response to water deprivation’, ‘response to osmotic stress’, ‘response to cold’, ‘regulation of stomatal movement’ and ‘transpiration’; hormone responses, such as ‘response to abscisic acid (ABA)’, ‘response to auxin’ and ‘response to brassinosteroid’, as well as ‘photosynthesis’ and ‘chlorophyll biosynthesis’ (Fig. 3h). Further EMSAs confirmed that EpTFIIAγ could bind to promoter regions of 387 wheat genes, underscoring its capacity to regulate diverse biological pathways in planta, such as those related to stress response, development, photosynthesis and yield formation (Extended Data Fig. 7a, Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Fig. 20).

Recent findings suggest that to define the regulatory network involved in the effects of EpTFIIAγ on photosynthetic efficiency, WUE and the drought-stress response, we compared transcriptomes of 20-day-old wild-type Fielder and EpTFIIAγ transgenic seedlings. This identified 1,953 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; fold change of more than 2 or less than 0.5, P < 0.05) in transgenic plants relative to Fielder, including 1,405 upregulated and 548 downregulated DEGs (Extended Data Fig. 7b–g and Supplementary Table 10). By examining overlap between ChIP–seq and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets, we identified 1,056 candidate target genes that are potentially bound and transcriptionally regulated by EpTFIIAγ, including 824 upregulated and 232 downregulated genes in EpTFIIAγ plants (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). Among them, stress-response-related genes involved in ABA and drought responses showed strong enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 8c), such as wheat homologues of Arabidopsis MYBR1 (ref. 30), FBH4 (ref. 31) and DREB1C32 (Supplementary Tables 9 and 10). Other genes known to function in plant development, source–sink partitioning and grain yield were also present among upregulated DEGs, including the CONSTANS-like gene TaCol-B5 (ref. 33), wheat homologues of rice OsCIN2 (ref. 34) and OsSWEET4 (ref. 35), and homologues of Arabidopsis VND7 (ref. 36) and SWEET12 (ref. 37). Among photosynthesis-related DEGs, we found TaYCF9 and TaCP47, which are homologues of Arabidopsis PsbZ38 and CP47 (ref. 39) encoding subunits of the PSII reaction centre. In addition, we identified TaCOG1, a homologue of the Arabidopsis Dof transcription factor COG1, that promotes biomass accumulation by enhancing photosynthetic capacity40. TaGAPC1, a redox-dependent regulator of energy metabolism that mediates stress responses in Arabidopsis41, was also upregulated (Supplementary Tables 9 and 10).

MBP–EpTFIIAγ could bind in vitro to approximately 30-bp promoter fragments containing TATA motifs from TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1, and this interaction could be compromised by competition from unlabelled probes (Fig. 3i, Extended Data Fig. 8d and Supplementary Fig. 21a). ChIP–quantitative PCR (qPCR) indicated that these promoter fragments demonstrated greater enrichment in EpTFIIAγ–HA genomic DNA precipitated by anti-haemagglutinin antibody than by the immunoglobulin G (IgG) control (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 8e), demonstrating that EpTFIIAγ could indeed bind to TATA-containing core promoter motifs. In dual-luciferase reporter assays using approximately 1.5-kb promoter fragments, activities of target promoters were upregulated in the presence of EpTFIIAγ compared with empty vector controls (Fig. 3k, Extended Data Fig. 8f and Supplementary Fig. 21b), supported by real-time (RT)–qPCR analyses revealing that TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1 mRNAs were all expressed at higher levels in all three EpTFIIAγ transgenic lines than in wild-type Fielder (Extended Data Fig. 8g). These results collectively indicated that EpTFIIAγ functions as a transcriptional cofactor to regulate target gene expression.

According to recent reports, to determine how downstream regulatory targets contribute to enhancing drought resistance, photosynthetic efficiency and grain yield in EpTFIIAγ plants, we generated transgenic wheat lines overexpressing TaDREB1C, TaCOG1 or TaCIN2 in the cv. Fielder background. TaDREB1C lines had enhanced drought resistance and WUE through accelerated stomatal closure and reduced transpiration compared with Fielder under drought stress (Extended Data Fig. 9a–g). This overexpression did not detectably alter growth period, which remained comparable with controls under full irrigation (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). Plants overexpressing TaCOG1 had enhanced photosynthetic and carbon-fixation capacities, resulting in increased biomass and grain yield relative to controls (Extended Data Fig. 9k–p). Moreover, TaCIN2 overexpression resulted in accelerated grain filling, ultimately increasing grain size and yield (Extended Data Fig. 9q–v). These results position the EpTFIIAγ regulon as pivotal for concurrently improving drought resilience and yield potential in wheat.

To investigate the mechanisms through which EpTFIIAγ drives enhanced drought resistance, photosynthetic capacity and grain yield, we conducted yeast two-hybrid screening using a cDNA library obtained from wheat cv. Chinese Spring seedlings. Four successive rounds of screening with EpTFIIAγ serving as bait yielded 112 candidate interacting proteins (Supplementary Table 11), including 22 putative transcription factors. After repeating yeast two-hybrid assays to confirm that EpTFIIAγ could interact with wheat homologues of Arabidopsis transcriptional activators WRKY46 (ref. 42), AKS1 (ref. 43), ARF6 (ref. 44) and VOZ1 (ref. 45) (Fig. 4a), luciferase-complementation imaging tested whether EpTFIIAγ could physically interact with these partners. Co-expression of EpTFIIAγ–C-terminal luciferase fragment (cLUC) with N-terminal luciferase fragment (nLUC)–TaWRKY46, nLUC–TaAKS1, nLUC–TaARF6 or nLUC–TaVOZ1 produced chemiluminescence, whereas no signal was observed in regions infiltrated with vector controls (Fig. 4b). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation assays further showed that co-expression of the EpTFIIAγ–cYFP with nYFP–TaWRKY46, nYFP–TaAKS1, nYFP–TaARF6 or nYFP–TaVOZ1 led to obvious YFP signal (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 22a,b). Pulldown assays indicated that MBP–EpTFIIAγ could interact with GST–TaWRKY46, GST–TaAKS1, GST–TaARF6 and HA–TaVOZ1 in vitro (Fig. 4d). Co-immunoprecipitation assays in N. benthamiana leaves co-expressing 35Spro:GFP–EpTFIIAγ and 35Spro:mCherry–TaWRKY46, 35Spro:mCherry–TaARF6 or 35Spro:mCherry–EpTFIIAγ with 35Spro:GFP–TaAKS1, 35Spro:GFP–TaVOZ1 also confirmed that EpTFIIAγ could physically interact with these transcription factors in planta (Fig. 4e). By contrast, the IDR-deleted EpTFIIAγ variant failed to detectably interact with any tested partners (Supplementary Fig. 22c,d), highlighting the essential role of this IDR. Moreover, no interactions were observed between wheat TaTFIIAγ and the transcription factors TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 or TaVOZ1 (Supplementary Fig. 22e,f), underscoring EpTFIIAγ functional specificity.

In a recent development, to map genome-wide binding sites and target genes, we used CUT&Tag in stable-transgenic cv. Fielder plants expressing TaWRKY46–HA, TaAKS1–FLAG, TaARF6–HA or TaVOZ1–HA. Integrative analysis identified 467, 309, 495 and 505 target genes that are potentially co-bound and co-regulated by EpTFIIAγ with TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 or TaVOZ1, respectively (Supplementary Table 12 and Supplementary Fig. 23), suggesting direct involvement in the EpTFIIAγ regulatory network. GST–TaWRKY46 could bind in vitro to probes containing the W-box from the TaCol-B5, TaSWEET4 and TaSWEET12 promoters, and these binding events increased in the presence of MBP–EpTFIIAγ (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Similarly, GST–TaAKS1 could bind to probes harbouring the G-box or E-box from the TaDREB1C, TaCol-B5, TaYCF9 or TaCOG1 promoter regions, with the addition of MBP–EpTFIIAγ markedly strengthening these interactions in vitro. Moreover, GST–TaARF6 could interact with AuxRE-containing probes derived from the TaYCF9, TaFBH4 and TaCIN2 promoters, which was boosted by addition of MBP–EpTFIIAγ, whereas GST–TaVOZ1 bound to probes with a 5′-CTTCTT-3′ motif present in the TaCP47, TaVND7, TaMYBR1 and TaGAPC1 promoter regions, which also increased in the presence of MBP–EpTFIIAγ (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a). Dual-luciferase reporter assays indicated that TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 could activate genes with corresponding promoter recognition sites (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10b).

Industry observers note that to determine whether EpTFIIAγ functions coordinately with or independently of TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 in regulating target genes, we performed dual-luciferase reporter assays. Upon co-expressing EpTFIIAγ with each respective transcription factor, LUC activity driven by the TaDREB1C, TaFBH4, TaMYBR1, TaVND7, TaCol-B5, TaCIN2, TaSWEET4, TaSWEET12, TaYCF9, TaCP47, TaCOG1 and TaGAPC1 promoters was greater than the expression of wheat transcription factors alone (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10b). To clarify whether activation of these transcription-factor genes contributed to the observed drought resistance of transgenic EpTFIIAγ plants, we examined drought resistance in lines overexpressing TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 (Extended Data Fig. 11a–d), as well as wrky46-knockout and arf6-knockout mutants by gene editing in cv. Fielder (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). All overexpression lines had enhanced drought resistance relative to Fielder, whereas both mutants had compromised drought resistance compared with Fielder controls (Extended Data Fig. 11g–j). To further characterize the genetic interactions of EpTFIIAγ with TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1, we crossed EpTFIIAγ plants (Fielder background) with each overexpression line. Under normal conditions, homozygous double-transgene-positive progeny of all crosses bore phenotypes comparable with that of TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 and TaVOZ1 overexpression plants. By contrast, double-transgene-carrying hybrids showed stronger drought resistance than control plants expressing a single transgene (Extended Data Fig. 11k,l). These findings collectively demonstrated that EpTFIIAγ physically interacts with select transcription activators, such as TaWRKY46, TaAKS1, TaARF6 or TaVOZ1, and that their interactions resulted in additive effects on EpTFIIAγ target gene expression, consequently enhancing the drought response, photosynthesis and grain yield.

To determine whether EpTFIIAγ function in conferring drought resistance was conserved in other major cereal crops, we generated three transgenic EpTFIIAγ lines each in rice cv. Nipponbare and maize inbred line B73 backgrounds (Fig. 5a,b). In greenhouse drought-resistance assays, survival of transgenic EpTFIIAγ rice and maize lines was extended by approximately 2.6-fold and approximately 2.8-fold for rice (Fig. 5c,d) and maize (Fig. 5e,f), respectively, compared with their wild-type controls. Transcriptomic analysis found that genes involved in ‘transcriptional regulation’, ‘response to ABA’, ‘response to water deprivation’, ‘response to osmotic stress’ and ‘photosynthesis’ were enriched among upregulated DEGs in EpTFIIAγ seedlings of both species (Extended Data Fig. 12a,b and Supplementary Tables 13 and 14).
